title: How Andy Burnham can get Brexit undone
gist: Labour peer Andrew Adonis argues, using the UK's 1961-73 EEC accession history, that rejoining the EU could be done within months to a few years if political will exists on both sides, but is impossible otherwise. He expects budget contributions and free movement to be the main sticking points, Euro and Schengen opt-outs to be settled politically, and a referendum to be a prerequisite.

insights.claim: Adonis argues historical precedent shows the UK could rejoin the EU very quickly—in months—if political will exists on both sides, but not at all if one side is opposed.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Rejoin timing is a function of political alignment, not technical complexity, so watch elections and EU leadership attitudes.
insights.quote: rejoining can be done very quickly—in a matter of months—if the political will exists on both sides of the negotiating table
insights.locator: The past is usually the best guide

insights.claim: The UK's first two EEC membership bids failed because Charles de Gaulle vetoed them for political reasons, not over trade detail or budget contributions.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Historical evidence that a single major member's veto, driven by leadership rivalry, can block UK accession.

insights.claim: After de Gaulle resigned in 1969, the UK under Edward Heath agreed a full accession treaty in only 19 months with backing from Pompidou and Brandt, and the whole joining process took barely two-and-a-half years.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Provides a benchmark timeline (~2.5 years) for a politically supported UK accession.
insights.quote: The whole process of joining took barely two-and-half years.

insights.claim: Adonis argues rejoining would be technically easier today than in the 1960s because UK trade and regulation remain closely aligned with the EU after nearly 50 years of membership and minimal post-Brexit divergence.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Low regulatory divergence keeps the option of rapid re-integration open, relevant to UK assets' long-term EU access premium.
insights.locator: Ah, but weren’t the issues simpler then

insights.claim: Whether the UK can opt out of the Euro and Schengen is a purely political decision that would likely be agreed as a statement of intent before formal negotiations begin.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: A rejoin scenario likely keeps sterling, limiting currency-union implications for UK markets.
insights.quote: This is a straightforwardly political decision.
insights.locator: As for the Euro and Schengen

insights.claim: Adonis expects the size of the UK's EU budget contribution to be the biggest bone of contention, with a gap of many billions and domestic media framing any figure as a sell-out.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Fiscal cost of rejoining will be the key domestic political battleground.
insights.quote: The biggest bone of contention will likely be the size of the British contribution to the EU budget.
insights.locator: That’s not to say that there won’t be

insights.claim: Adonis argues free movement is unlikely to be a deal-breaker because Poles and eastern Europeans are less inclined to work abroad now their economies have radically strengthened, and a long phasing-in could be negotiated.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Reduced migration pressure from eastern Europe lowers a key political barrier to UK-EU reintegration.
insights.locator: Free movement of people will be another

insights.claim: Adonis suggests a Rejoin government should mobilise British tourists and business travellers frustrated by post-Brexit travel and residence bureaucracy to argue free movement benefits Britons too.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Travel friction is a potential pro-EU political lever, relevant to travel and mobility sectors.
insights.locator: The benefits of the EU dropping

insights.claim: Adonis believes both an election and a referendum would almost certainly be required before any Rejoin deal is negotiated, partly because EU leaders would demand a decisive British mandate.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Rejoin is a multi-year, multi-vote process, so near-term market impact is limited.
insights.quote: A referendum, as well as an election, would almost certainly be required before any Rejoin deal could be negotiated.
insights.locator: However, one point seems fairly clear

insights.claim: Adonis notes the idea of rejoining is gathering steam and that continental views of Britain remain benign, bolstered by joint support for Ukraine, with the real question being political will in five to 10 years.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Improving UK-EU relations raise the probability of closer economic integration over a 5-10 year horizon.
insights.locator: I obviously can’t supply an answer

insights.claim: Winning a Rejoin referendum requires a UK government firmly committed to Rejoin and EU partners willing to outline a deal including Euro and Schengen opt-outs, leaving Andy Burnham's tentative options far from that point.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Monitor whether a Burnham-led Labour shifts from tentative closer-ties options to an explicit Rejoin commitment.
insights.locator: For a Rejoin referendum to be won
